doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Jack Lawrence's song Linda and Henry Mancini visiting the hotel gig
summary: Anecdote of the song Linda, written in 1946 and later linked to Paul McCartney, then Henry Mancini hearing Weber play his obscure songs at a hotel.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Are you familiar with the composer Jack Lawrence?

Jack Lawrence wrote a string of pop hits in the forties, fifties, sixties, anyway, one of which he wrote for his friends John and Louise Eastman and their daughter Linda, who was about kindergarten age. This was 1946. He wrote a song for the kid. Oh, how does it go? Her name is Linda. “When I go to sleep/I never count sheep/I count all the charms about Linda. Lately it seems/in all my dreams/I dream with my arms about Linda. You’ve heard that song perhaps?

A whole bunch of Lindas. They listen to the song, oh that’s nice, and you can hear a cash register ringing. Lo and behold they did release it and it became a — Buddy Clark sang it, an enormous hit and it was on the hit parade at least two months, it was top of the charts a bunch of that time. Tons of girls named Linda after that. All right fast forward. The girl for whom that song was written, Linda, March 12, 1969 guess what she does?

Exactly. So, he owns that song. He bought the rights to that song. Now if Paul McCartney wanders in, what do you give him? You give him “Linda.” So in any case, Henry Mancini walks in what do you give him? It’s hard to lay in all these tunes on him from his film scores that he thought, “Who knows this?” He even at one point, he’s got his arms crossed and he’s kind of half-smiling at me, what a great guy he was. April 16, 1924, I observe his birthday. In any case, and June 14, 1984, his death. But he said, “Come here a second, how old are you?” I said, “25.” He said, “How do you know so many of my songs?” I said, “Well you’re a famous guy. Of course I know these songs.” “And what was that second to the last one?” “Oh that was ‘Blue Sad’ and you did that with Jay Livingston and Ray Evans, guys who were born six weeks apart in 1950.” And he loved it. He loved it, and we started laughing about some of it, and he said, “Oh yeah, that was in the ‘Mr. Lucky’ TV show, you remember?” And he said “yeah, I do. We wrote those in five minutes sometimes.” Anyway, how we got on Henry Mancini, I’m trying to remember how we —
